turns.prompt_text: There's some guy who who has researched ants and knows a very good amount about ants. He passed away recently, maybe a few years ago. I think his name is William or Wilson or Emerson
turns.response_html:
You are definitely thinking of E.O. Wilson (Edward Osborne Wilson). He was a world-renowned biologist, naturalist, and writer who was widely considered the world's leading authority on ants.

Often nicknamed "The Ant Man," he passed away on December 26, 2021, at the age of 92.

Wilson was a professor at Harvard for decades and made massive contributions to science, including:

  • Myrmecology: The formal study of ants. He discovered hundreds of new species and figured out how ants communicate using chemical trails (pheromones).
  • Sociobiology: He pioneered this field, which looks at the genetic basis for social behaviors in animals (like ants, bees, and eventually humans).
  • Biodiversity Advocacy: Later in life, he became a massive voice for global conservation, introducing the "Half-Earth" project, which proposes setting aside half of the Earth's land and sea for nature to stop the mass extinction of species.
  • Pulitzer Prizes: He didn't just write academic papers; he was an incredible writer who won two Pulitzer Prizes for General Nonfiction (one of them specifically for his massive book The Ants).

He famously once said, "Most children have a bug period. I never grew out of mine."

turns.prompt_text: What all does he know about ants?
turns.response_html:
E.O. Wilson practically rewrote our entire understanding of how ants live, think, and interact. Because he spent over 80 years studying them, he didn't just know random facts—he mapped out their entire civilization.

If you look into what he discovered, it essentially breaks down into four major areas:

1. The Pheromone "Language"

Before Wilson, people knew ants were highly coordinated, but they didn’t really understand how they did it. Wilson figured out that ants live in a completely chemical world.

  • The Fire Ant Experiment: He discovered that an ant's Dufour’s gland secretes a fluid that acts as a directional guide. He actually took a gland from a dead fire ant, drew a fake trail with it on a glass plate, and watched hundreds of live ants mindlessly follow his inkless pen line.
  • The Vocabulary: He proved that ants have about 10 to 20 different "chemical words." By sweeping their sensitive antennae through the air, they can instantly taste or smell whether a pheromone trail means "Food this way," "Quick, defend the nest!" (alarm), or "This is what our specific colony smells like."

2. The Mechanics of the "Superorganism"

Wilson popularized the idea that a single ant doesn't really act as an individual; instead, the entire colony operates together as a single, massive organism—a superorganism.

  • The Caste System: He deeply researched how an ant's genetics and diet dictate its physical body and role. He tracked how colonies divide labor perfectly among tiny "nurse" ants, specialized foragers, and massive "soldier" ants with huge mandibles.
  • Aggressive Warfare: He famously wrote about how ants are the most warlike creatures on Earth, noting that their massive colony battles completely dwarf human historical battles like Waterloo. He even observed that colonies will send their oldest, weakest worker ants out to the front lines of a war zone because they are the most expendable.

3. Leafcutters and the First Farmers

Wilson did extensive work on leafcutter ants, revealing that they are some of the only non-human creatures on Earth to invent agriculture. He showed how they don't actually eat the leaves they cut down; instead, they haul the leaves deep underground, chew them into a paste, and use that compost to cultivate a highly specific, specialized fungus. The ants then eat the fungus.

4. Discovering and Cataloging Species

Wilson was an elite taxonomist (someone who discovers and names species).

  • He discovered and officially described over 400 new species of ants during his expeditions across the South Pacific, the Amazon, and the American South.
  • As a 13-year-old kid growing up in Alabama, he actually discovered and reported the very first colony of invasive imported fire ants ever recorded on United States soil.

He co-wrote a massive, 700-page academic textbook simply titled The Ants. It is so extraordinarily detailed that it remains the ultimate "bible" of ant biology to this day, and it is the only textbook of its kind to ever win a Pulitzer Prize.

turns.prompt_text: What is the story of how E.O. Wilson became interested in insects and ants when he was a kid?
turns.response_html:
The origin story of E.O. Wilson's obsession with ants is actually a fascinating mix of childhood loneliness, a series of physical limitations, and a freak fishing accident.

It proves that sometimes our greatest constraints end up defining our life's purpose.

1. Finding Refuge in Nature

Wilson grew up in the American South during the Great Depression. His parents divorced when he was seven years old, and because his father’s job required constant moving, Wilson attended 14 different schools in 11 years.

With no long-term friends and an unstable home life, he turned to the woods, swamps, and beaches of Alabama and Florida for comfort. He became a solitary "boy naturalist," spending hours exploring by himself.

2. The Freak Accident

When he was 7 years old, he was fishing off a dock in Florida. He yanked a pinfish out of the water a little too hard, and the fish flew directly into his face. One of its sharp dorsal spines struck his right eye, puncturing the pupil.

Because of medical delays and a poorly executed surgery a few months later, a traumatic cataract developed, leaving him completely blind in his right eye for the rest of his life.

3. The Physical Constraints That Chose His Destiny

As he grew older, Wilson's physical challenges mounted:

  • Blind in one eye: He lacked stereoscopic vision (depth perception), meaning he couldn't easily spot birds in flight or track fast-moving mammals through binoculars.
  • Hearing loss: In his teenage years, he lost the ability to hear high-frequency sounds, which meant he couldn't hear bird calls or frog chirps.

But his left eye had a unique superpower: it possessed unusually sharp, close-up vision. He later noted that he could read the fine print on a dollar bill without glasses well into adulthood.

Because he couldn't look up into the trees at birds, he looked down. He realized he was perfectly physically adapted to look at the tiny, intricate details of objects right in front of his face. He decided to focus entirely on insects.

4. Why Ants?

At age 9, he read a National Geographic article titled "Stalking Ants for Savage Slams," which romanticized the complex society and intense battle strategies of ants. He was completely hooked.

By the time he was 13, living in a neighborhood in Mobile, Alabama, he began cataloging local insects. Right outside his doorstep in a vacant lot, he discovered a massive, aggressive colony of ants he had never seen before. He documented them meticulously.

Years later, scientists confirmed that a 13-year-old E.O. Wilson had officially discovered the very first colony of invasive Imported Fire Ants (Solenopsis invicta) in the United States—the exact species that would later spread across the entire American South and become a major focus of his early research.
